lesson.title: Before You Say Yes: Admission Control and the Limits of a Promise
lesson.summary: Admission control is the check a network performs before accepting a new flow's request for guaranteed resources, refusing new demand outright whenever granting it would break promises already made to existing traffic.
lesson.body:
The telephone network's old busy signal is a useful mental model for what admission control is trying to do. A traditional phone network had a fixed number of trunk lines available at any given point, and a call attempted when every trunk was already in use simply got a busy signal, rather than being connected anyway into a call so degraded neither party could actually talk. That is the core idea admission control carries over into packet networks: it is often better for a network to say no cleanly, up front, than to accept every request and quietly let everyone's quality degrade below what was actually promised.

More formally, admission control takes a resource reservation request from a new flow, described using parameters shaped just like the r and b of a token bucket covered earlier, together with a picture of how much capacity is already committed to every flow admitted before it, and computes whether the remaining capacity along the relevant path can satisfy the new request without violating any guarantee already made. If the answer is yes, the flow is admitted and its resources are set aside. If the answer is no, the request is rejected outright, before any packets are ever sent under a false promise.

This concept is really only fully meaningful in the context of the next major architecture covered in this unit, Integrated Services. Admission control is the specific gatekeeping step that every router along a path performs when RSVP signaling asks it to reserve resources for a flow. It is also the reason IntServ is described as reservation-based in any serious sense: without an admission control check at each hop, a reservation would just be an unenforced request, and any flow could claim resources that the network cannot actually deliver.

It is worth contrasting this directly with what the next chapter's architecture, DiffServ, does not do. DiffServ traffic classes describe relative treatment, one class gets handled better than another, but DiffServ typically involves no per-flow admission check at all. An operator instead provisions capacity for each traffic class in advance based on expected or measured aggregate demand, rather than checking every individual flow at connection time. That provisioned, statistical approach is a major reason DiffServ is able to scale to the size of the real internet, where per-flow admission control, as will become clear in the IntServ chapter, simply cannot.
